test_text.title: Whatever happened to the Harappan Civilisation?

article.title: Whatever happened to the Harappan Civilisation?

items.sentence_raw: The Harappan Civilisation of ancient Pakistan and India flourished 5,000 years ago, but a thousand years later their cities were abandoned.

The Harappan Civilisation was a sophisticated Bronze Age society who built 'megacities' and traded internationally in luxury craft products, and yet seemed to have left almost no depictions of themselves.
But their lack of self-imagery - at a time when the Egyptians were carving and painting representations of themselves all over their temples - is only part of the mystery.
items.explain: Q29: The question wants a **'difference'** between the Harappan Civilisation and **'another culture of the same period'**. The passage mentions the Harappans had a *'lack of self-imagery'* — they did not make pictures of themselves. But at the same time, *'the Egyptians were carving and painting representations of themselves all over their temples'*. This is a clear contrast between two cultures. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: "There is plenty of archaeological evidence to tell us about the rise of the Harappan Civilisation, but relatively little about its fall," explains archaeologist Dr Cameron Petrie of the University of Cambridge.
items.explain: Q40: The statement says information about the decline has been **'lacking'** — missing. The passage quotes Petrie saying there is *'relatively little about its fall'*. **'Relatively little'** means lacking, and **'fall'** means decline. So the answer is **A**.

items.sentence_raw: "As populations increased, cities were built that had great baths, craft workshops, palaces and halls laid out in distinct sectors.
items.explain: Q30: The question asks for **'features of Harappan urban design'** — how their cities were built. The passage describes cities with *'great baths, craft workshops, palaces and halls laid out in distinct sectors'*, and houses *'arranged in blocks, with wide main streets and narrow alleyways'*, plus *'their own wells and drainage systems'*. These are all design features. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Houses were arranged in blocks, with wide main streets and narrow alleyways, and many had their own wells and drainage systems.
items.explain: Q30: The question asks for **'features of Harappan urban design'** — how their cities were built. The passage describes cities with *'great baths, craft workshops, palaces and halls laid out in distinct sectors'*, and houses *'arranged in blocks, with wide main streets and narrow alleyways'*, plus *'their own wells and drainage systems'*. These are all design features. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: It was very much a 'thriving' civilisation."
Then around 2100 BC, a transformation began.
Streets went uncleaned, buildings started to be abandoned, and ritual structures fell out of use.
After their final demise, a millennium passed before really large-scale cities appeared once more in South Asia.

Some have claimed that major glacier-fed rivers changed their course, dramatically affecting the water supply and agriculture; or that the cities could not cope with an increasing population, they exhausted their resource base, the trading economy broke down or they succumbed to invasion and conflict; and yet others that climate change caused an environmental change that affected food and water provision.
items.explain: Q27: Many students get confused because the question asks for **'proposed explanations'** — this means ideas people have suggested, not proven facts. The passage lists several ideas: *'major glacier-fed rivers changed their course'*, *'cities could not cope with an increasing population'*, *'trading economy broke down'*, and *'climate change caused an environmental change'*. All these are possible reasons for the decline. So the answer is **C**.

items.sentence_raw: "It is unlikely that there was a single cause for the decline of the civilisation.
But the fact is, until now, we have had little solid evidence from the area for most of the key elements," said Petrie.
"A lot of the archaeological debate has really only been well-argued speculation."

A research team led by Petrie, together with Dr Ravindanath Singh of Banaras Hindu University in India, found early in their investigations that many of the archaeological sites were not where they were supposed to be, completely altering understanding of the way that this region was inhabited in the past.

When they carried out a survey of how the larger area was settled in relation to sources of water, they found inaccuracies in the published geographic locations of ancient settlements ranging from several hundred metres to many kilometres.
items.explain: Q31: The question mentions **'errors made by previous archaeologists'** — mistakes in old work. The passage says researchers *'found inaccuracies in the published geographic locations of ancient settlements ranging from several hundred metres to many kilometres'*. **'Inaccuracies'** means errors, and these were in published data from earlier work. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: They realised that any attempts to use the existing data were likely to be fundamentally flawed.
Over the course of several seasons of fieldwork they carried out new surveys, finding an astonishing 198 settlement sites that were previously unknown.

Now, research published by Dr Yama Dixit and Professor David Hodell, both from Cambridge's Department of Earth Sciences, has provided the first definitive evidence for climate change affecting the plains of north-western India, where hundreds of Harappan sites are known to have been situated.
The researchers gathered shells of "Melanoides tuberculata" snails from the sediments of an ancient lake and used geochemical analysis as a means of tracing the climate history of the region.
items.explain:
Q32: The question says they collected something from snails. The passage says researchers *'gathered shells of "Melanoides tuberculata" snails'*. **'Gathered'** means collected, so the thing they collected is **'shells'**. So the answer is **shells**.

Q33: The question asks where they found evidence of a change in water levels. The passage says they took snail shells *'from the sediments of an ancient lake'*. The water level change happened in this **'lake'**. So the answer is **lake**.

items.sentence_raw: "As today, the major source of water into the lake is likely to have been the summer monsoon," says Dixit.
"But we have observed that there was an abrupt change about 4,100 years ago, when the amount of evaporation from the lake exceeded the rainfall - indicative of a drought."
items.explain: Q34: The question says there was less of something than evaporation. The passage explains *'the amount of evaporation from the lake exceeded the rainfall'*. **'Exceeded'** means was more than — so evaporation was more than **'rainfall'**, meaning there was less rainfall. So the answer is **rainfall**.

items.sentence_raw: Hodell adds: "We estimate that the weakening of the Indian summer monsoon climate lasted about 200 years before recovering to the previous conditions, which we still see today."
items.explain: Q39: The statement mentions **'rough calculations'** of the length of a water shortage. The passage quotes Hodell saying *'We estimate that the weakening of the Indian summer monsoon climate lasted about 200 years'*. **'Estimate'** means a rough calculation, and 200 years is the length. So the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: It has long been thought that other great Bronze Age civilisations also declined at a similar time, with a global-scale climate event being seen as the cause.

While it is possible that these local-scale processes were linked, the real archaeological interest lies in understanding the impact of these larger-scale events on different environments and different populations.

"Considering the vast area of the Harappan Civilisation with its variable weather systems," explains Singh, "it is essential that we obtain more climate data from areas close to the two great cities at Mohenjodaro and Harappa and also from the Indian Punjab."
items.explain: Q37: The statement says finding more climate information is **'vital'** — very important. The passage quotes Singh saying *'it is essential that we obtain more climate data'*. **'Essential'** means vital, so this matches Singh. So the answer is **B**.

items.sentence_raw: Petrie and Singh's team is now examining archaeological records and trying to understand details of how people led their lives in the region five millennia ago.

They are analysing grains cultivated at the time, and trying to work out whether they were grown under extreme conditions of water stress, and whether they were adjusting the combinations of crops they were growing for different weather systems.
items.explain: Q35: The question asks what they are looking at from five millennia ago to understand farming. The passage says *'They are analysing grains cultivated at the time'*. **'Cultivated'** means grown, and these **'grains'** are from five millennia ago. So the answer is **grains**.

items.sentence_raw: They are also looking at whether the types of pottery used, and other aspects of their material culture, were distinctive to specific regions or were more similar across larger areas.
items.explain: Q36: The question asks about objects they examine to find links between regions. The passage says they look at *'whether the types of pottery used... were distinctive to specific regions or were more similar across larger areas'*. **'Pottery'** is the object that shows connections. So the answer is **pottery**.

items.sentence_raw: This gives us insight into the types of interactive networks that the population was involved in, and whether those changed.
Petrie believes that archaeologists are in a unique position to investigate how past societies responded to environmental and climatic change.

"By investigating responses to environmental pressures and threats, we can learn from the past to engage with the public, and the relevant governmental and administrative bodies, to be more proactive in issues such as the management and administration of water supply, the balance of urban and rural development, and the importance of preserving cultural heritage in the future."
items.explain:
Q28: The question asks for a **'present-day application'** — how the research can be used now. The passage says we can *'learn from the past to engage with the public, and the relevant governmental and administrative bodies, to be more proactive in issues such as the management and administration of water supply'*. This directly connects old research to modern problem-solving. So the answer is **H**.

Q38: The statement says examining past behaviour may have **'long-term benefits'**. The passage quotes Petrie saying we can *'learn from the past to engage with the public... to be more proactive in issues such as the management and administration of water supply'* — this is a long-term benefit for the future. So the answer is **A**.

subtitles: New research sheds light on the disappearance of an ancient society
